小鼓屬膜鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs編號211.212.11，源自歐: The snare drum is a membranophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 211.212.11, and comes from the medieval European tabor, which was first used to accompany the flute. The tabor later gave rise to types such as the drum-kit snare, the marching snare, the tarol, the soprano snare and the piccolo snare, differing in size and playing style. The modern snare drum is common in the orchestra, the concert band, the marching band, on parade, in drum lines and drum corps, and it is the core instrument of the drum kit. In popular music it usually plays on the second and fourth beats, or off the beat on the third at slow tempos; in marching bands the snare drummers play only the snare, often using accented patterns of semiquavers and triplet quavers that make the playing more intricate. Because the basic rhythm is easy to learn, it is also used in children's music education and rhythm ensembles.

It is very responsive, so it can be tapped lightly with brushes or struck hard for an accent; striking rim and head together gives a metallic accent, and striking the rim at the side gives a dry, high note. With the snares disengaged the timbre is close to a floor tom. Pitch and volume depend on the material, tension and size of the heads and on the shell, and the piccolo snare is higher in pitch.

The snare drum is a European membranophone percussion instrument, Hornbostel–Sachs 211.212.11. It has a top and a bottom head, with a set of snares lying against the bottom head; when the top head is struck with a stick, brushes, rutes or the hands, the bottom head vibrates and sets the snares going, producing a short, crisp sound. The snares can be engaged or disengaged with a strainer, and when disengaged the timbre is close to a floor tom. The snare drum is common in the orchestra, the concert band, the marching band, on parade, in drum lines and drum corps, and it is one of the core instruments of the drum kit.
